analysis.one_liner: Requires banks to get customers' written consent before charging overdraft fees and bans reordering transactions to trigger them.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Financial Services Committee and a subcommittee until the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Banks were charging fees when customers spent more than was in their accounts — sometimes deliberately posting the largest debits first so more transactions overdraw at once. This bill would have required customers to sign up in writing before a bank could charge overdraft fees on ATM and debit transactions, made ATMs show the real account balance and warn before a fee, restricted ads that pitch 'free' accounts carrying steep overdraft fees, and banned manipulating the order of transactions to generate fees. It also directed the Federal Reserve to study how these programs work and how much they cost consumers.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank customers, especially people living close to zero in their accounts, who bore the brunt of overdraft fees — often low- and moderate-income households hit repeatedly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bank customers living paycheck to paycheck

how_it_helps.text: No bank could charge an overdraft fee on ATM withdrawals or electronic transactions unless the customer had affirmatively requested the service in writing [S3].

ATMs operated by the bank would have to show only the actual dollar balance — not an inflated figure that includes phantom overdraft 'protection' — and warn the customer before completing a transaction that would trigger a fee [S3].
The bill barred a pattern or practice of delaying deposits or manipulating the order in which checks and debits are posted in order to cause overdrafts and collect fees [S3].
It banned misleading advertising — for example, calling an account 'free' when it carries overdraft fees, or promising to honor all checks when the bank keeps discretion to bounce them [S3].

Overdraft fees would have counted as finance charges under the Truth in Lending Act, so their true annualized cost had to be disclosed, and the Federal Reserve would have to study these programs and report to Congress within a year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Depository institutions — banks and thrifts — which collected billions in overdraft fee revenue, plus the third-party vendors that ran their overdraft programs for a cut.

drawbacks.text: Banks argued that covering an overdraft is a service: the transaction gets paid instead of bouncing, sparing the customer a returned-item fee from the merchant and the embarrassment of a declined card. Under the bill, fees on occasional courtesy coverage (up to three per year) were still allowed, but the blanket consent requirement would have cut off automatic coverage many customers liked [S3].

The bill added detailed written agreements, per-transaction ATM notices, and periodic-statement disclosures, which banks said would raise compliance costs and add friction to routine transactions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For customers repeatedly hit with $20-to-$35 fees on small purchases — the people overdraft programs actually cost the most — the protections outweighed the added friction, since the bill preserved true opt-in services and linked-account transfers. For customers who rarely overdrafted and valued silent coverage of the occasional shortfall, the consent requirement was a mild inconvenience. The core tradeoff: banks would lose a large, opaque fee revenue stream; consumers would gain transparency and control.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to its subcommittee on financial institutions, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Represent Carolyn Maloney of New York introduced the bill on July 27, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1][S5].
Fourteen members cosponsored it — 13 Democrats and 1 Independent; no Republican signed on [S4].
On August 24, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, which is where bills typically go to die quietly [S5].
The action record shows nothing after that referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor action — through the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and third-party overdraft vendors kept collecting overdraft fees with no consent requirement, no ban on reordering transactions, and no change to their advertising, for more than a decade longer.

for.name: Rep. Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the House.

for.name: 14 cosponsors (13 House Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Reps. Bernie Sanders, Barney Frank, and Barbara Lee as original cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it went to a subcommittee and stayed there.

against.name: Banking industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on overdraft fee practices, which had become a major and growing source of bank fee revenue.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders, with no Republican support recorded; the Republican-controlled committee took no action on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: Overdraft fees were a large, largely invisible revenue stream collected disproportionately from customers with low balances. The bill would have required consent, disclosure of the true balance, and honest advertising, directly cutting that revenue.

Banks commonly outsourced overdraft programs to vendors paid based on fee revenue; the bill's study mandate specifically flagged this compensation structure as a consumer risk. Restrictions on fees would have undercut the whole business model.
